title: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 AI and Culture in Spring 2026
author: Alexander, Bryan
summary: This horizon scan surveys cultural responses to generative AI across four domains in spring 2026: AI as cultural artifact, AI for storytelling, the companionbot movement, and public attitudes. The volume of AI-generated content continues to grow across ebooks, songs, scholarly papers, and web pages. In cinema, a full feature film entered Cannes competition at under $500K total production cost; director Paul Schrader predicts film school students will be producing full narratives solo on zero budget within a year. Companionbots appear durable: academic research finds Replika users rating AI companions as emotionally comparable to humans, and physical AI-backed robots are entering senior care settings. Attitude data reveals a striking paradox: the United States is simultaneously the world's foremost developer of AI and the most anti-AI nation in Pew's global survey. Quinnipiac polling finds 80% of Americans concerned about AI and 55% believing it will do more harm than good in their daily lives. Grass-roots data center opposition has already blocked at least 48 projects valued at $156 billion, constituting an emerging AI populism. The author anticipates a deepening partisan AI divide and expects the cultural opposition to intensify as AI capability continues to advance.
points: * AI-generated cultural content is growing across all media types; a feature film produced for under $500K entered Cannes competition, and a filmmaker predicts solo zero-budget narratives within a year. * Companionbots appear durable: Replika users report emotional connections comparable to human relationships, and physical AI-backed robots are entering senior care settings as social companions. * The United States is simultaneously the world's foremost AI developer and its most anti-AI nation by Pew data—a structural contradiction that shapes the broader cultural discourse. * 80% of Americans are concerned about AI and 55% believe it will do more harm than good; GenZ leads all cohorts in expecting AI to reduce job opportunities (81%). * Grass-roots data center opposition has blocked or delayed 48 projects worth $156 billion, constituting an emerging AI populism organized through local protests and political lobbying.
quotes: The sheer amount of AI content continues to grow across many cultural fields. The number of ebooks, songs, scholarly papers, and web pages with some or all content created by AI keeps on rising.
America is both the world's foremost developer of AI and its chief hater.

Just over one-third of Americans (35 percent) are either very excited (6 percent) or somewhat excited (29 percent) about AI, while 62 percent are either not so excited (29 percent) or not excited at all (33 percent).
Eighty percent are either very concerned (38 percent) or somewhat concerned (42 percent) about AI, while 18 percent are either not so concerned (10 percent) or not concerned at all (8 percent).

An overwhelming majority (81 percent) say they would prefer to rely on a combination of both AI and a human, 14 percent say they would prefer to rely solely on information provided by a human, and 3 percent say they would prefer to rely solely on information provided by AI.
I'm expecting more Democrats to oppose AI, while Republicans maintain their support for it, and AI becomes another partisan, culture wars front or signifier.
